sources.title: Meiosis
sources.publisher: Garland Science, hosted on NCBI Bookshelf
sources.version: Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition, chapter section NBK26840
sources.locator: Sections on the two meiotic divisions, homolog pairing, chiasmata in segregation, and genetic reassortment: homologs defined; bivalent of four chromatids; one replication then two divisions; duplicated homologs separate at anaphase I, sister chromatids at anaphase II; chiasmata hold homologs until anaphase I and pairs lacking them missegregate; arm cohesins degraded at start of anaphase I, centromeric ones at division II; 2^n assortment, at least 2^23 in humans; non-disjunction defined.
sources.license: Conventional copyright, 2002 Alberts, Johnson, Lewis, Raff, Roberts and Walter; facts-only use with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the definition of a homolog, the bivalent and its four chromatids, the single replication followed by two divisions, what separates at each anaphase, the mechanical role of the chiasma and the consequence of its absence, the two-stage degradation of arm and centromeric cohesins, the 2-to-the-n rule for independent assortment with its human value, and the definition and consequence of non-disjunction. No wording, figure, table, dataset or example was copied or adapted. The counting argument for why two divisions are required, the explicit chromosome-against-chromatid bookkeeping, the reading of arm-cohesion release as what resolves the chiasma, and every arithmetical step in the lesson are the lesson's own.

sources.title: Cytological Studies of Human Meiosis: Sex-Specific Differences in Recombination Originate at, or Prior to, Establishment of Double-Strand Breaks
sources.version: Volume 8, issue 12, article e85075; DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0085075; PMID 24376867
sources.locator: Results: mean MLH1 foci 49.09 (SE 0.07) per cell in males from 4660 spermatocytes, 69.25 (SE 0.29) in females from 2038 oocytes, across 56 testicular biopsies and 63 fetal ovaries; RAD51 foci 134.07 (SE 5.47) from 44 spermatocytes, 250.28 (SE 10.21) from 39 oocytes; bivalents lacking an MLH1 focus 0.38 per cent male against 2.60 per cent female; genetic lengths the authors calculated as 2455 cM male and 3463 cM female, with their note that linkage studies report longer maps.
sources.license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License, as declared on the article page); used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the measured crossover-marker and break-marker counts per cell in each sex with their standard errors and sample sizes, the frequency of bivalents lacking a crossover marker in each sex, and the genome-wide genetic map lengths the authors calculated together with their own caveat about linkage studies. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. The division of the genome-wide counts by 23 to obtain a per-bivalent figure, the application of the 50 cM conversion as a check that then exposes the two numbers as non-independent, and the estimate of switch points carried by a single gamete are the lesson's own arithmetic.

sources.title: Inefficient Crossover Maturation Underlies Elevated Aneuploidy in Human Female Meiosis
sources.locator: Results on crossovers, precursors and maturation efficiency: double-strand breaks about 200 per nucleus in males, about 400 in females; crossovers about 50 and about 70 per nucleus; coefficient of variation of crossover number per nucleus 18 per cent female against 10 per cent male; about 25 per cent of designated crossover interactions in the female never mature, efficiency about 0.75 against about 1.0 in the male; zero-crossover bivalents more frequent in female for every chromosome measured.
sources.license: NIH Public Access author manuscript deposited in PMC; used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the higher double-strand-break estimates per nucleus in each sex, the cell-to-cell coefficient of variation of crossover number in each sex, the proportion of designated crossover precursors that fail to mature in the female against the male, and the direction of the difference in zero-crossover bivalent frequency. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. The use of these figures to resolve the failed prediction in scene 3, which the lesson sets up and then answers, is the lesson's own construction; the source does not present that argument.

sources.title: Human aneuploidy: mechanisms and new insights into an age-old problem
sources.version: Volume 13, issue 7, pages 493-504; DOI 10.1038/nrg3245; PMID 22705668; author manuscript NIHMS423265
sources.locator: Sections on recombination, sex differences and maternal age: aneuploid embryos at least 10 per cent of pregnancies, possibly over 50 per cent near the end of reproductive lifespan; about 0.3 per cent of newborns, about 35 per cent of spontaneous abortions; most aneuploidies maternal; stage inferred from centromeric heterozygosity or homozygosity; over 10 per cent of oocytes carry a crossover-less bivalent; J-shaped curve read as multiple mechanisms; cohesin loss unlikely to be the only force.
sources.license: Author manuscript in PMC, 2012 Macmillan Publishers Limited, all rights reserved; used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the population frequencies of aneuploidy in pregnancies, newborns and spontaneous abortions, the maternal predominance, the centromeric-marker method for assigning a meiotic stage, the contribution of recombination failure with the proportion of oocytes carrying a crossover-less bivalent, the J-shaped age curve and its interpretation as evidence of multiple mechanisms, and the authors' explicit judgment that cohesin loss is unlikely to be the sole driver. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. The status table in scene 6 that separates documented findings from open questions is the lesson's own synthesis of this review with the two studies cited beside it.

sources.title: Advanced maternal age and the risk of Down syndrome characterized by the meiotic stage of chromosomal error: a population-based study
sources.locator: Results and discussion, 170 infants with trisomy 21, Atlanta 1989-1993, origin by DNA polymorphisms: 86 per cent maternal (75 per cent meiosis I, 25 per cent meiosis II), 9 per cent paternal split evenly, 5 per cent mitotic; women 40 and over against under 25, odds ratio 5.2 for maternal meiosis I and 51.4 for maternal meiosis II; authors conclude an association with both divisions, that meiosis I does not pinpoint timing, and that meiosis II implies a mechanism acting near conception.
sources.license: Archived journal content in PMC under the PMC copyright notice; used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the cohort size and ascertainment, the distribution of trisomy 21 by parental origin and meiotic stage, the two stage-specific odds ratios for the oldest against the youngest maternal age band, and the authors' own three-part conclusion about what the association does and does not establish. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. The derivation of roughly 37 maternal meiosis II cases from the reported percentages, and the use of that number to bound confidence in the size of the 51.4 odds ratio, are the lesson's own arithmetic and are labelled as such in the scene.

sources.title: Chromosome errors in human eggs shape natural fertility over reproductive life span
creators: Eva R. Hoffmann and 24 further co-authors
sources.locator: Results on error classes and age, 218 oocytes and 5014 chromosomes from donors aged 9 to 43: aneuploidy follows a U-shaped relation with age; three classes, meiosis I non-disjunction as whole-chromosome gain or loss, precocious separation of sister chromatids at meiosis I, and reverse segregation with both homologs splitting sisters at meiosis I; non-disjunction fell with age while the other two rose; cohesion weakening proposed as a molecular clock; the young-age mechanism stated to be unclear.
sources.license: Author manuscript deposited in PMC; used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the cohort size and age range, the U-shaped relation between aneuploidy and age, the definitions of the three error classes, the opposite age trends of those classes, the authors' molecular-clock proposal presented here as a proposal, and their explicit statement that the mechanism behind elevated meiosis I non-disjunction in young females is currently unclear. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. This source was checked specifically for whether it states that these error patterns would be misclassified by centromere-marker studies; it does not, and the lesson therefore makes no such claim and says so in the relevant source note.

sources.title: Regulation of the meiotic divisions of mammalian oocytes and eggs
sources.locator: Sections on oocyte arrest and the two divisions: oocytes form from primordial germ cells in the fetal ovary, commit one-way into meiosis, arrest at the germinal-vesicle stage comparable to somatic G2, and spend most of their life having entered meiosis without completing it; the first division is very asymmetric, giving a mature egg and a much smaller first polar body; the egg re-arrests at metaphase II until fertilisation; the meiosis I spindle checkpoint appears weak.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution License, as declared on the article page); used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the formation of oocytes in the fetal ovary and their arrest before completing meiosis, the asymmetry of both meiotic divisions with a first and a second polar body, the re-arrest at metaphase of meiosis II and its release by fertilisation, and the weakness of the spindle assembly checkpoint during oocyte meiosis I. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. This source describes two polar bodies; the lesson reports two on that basis and explicitly records its disagreement with accounts giving three, rather than reconciling them silently.

sources.title: Leagues of their own: sexually dimorphic features of meiotic prophase I
sources.locator: Sections contrasting oogenesis and spermatogenesis: mammalian oogenesis occurs during fetal development with oocytes arrested in late prophase I for decades, while spermatogenesis occurs throughout the lifespan; oogenesis divides asymmetrically with half the genome segregated into polar bodies, producing a single viable gamete, while spermatogenesis divides symmetrically producing four; spermatogenesis checkpoints are stringent with errors extremely rare, the oogenesis response very poor.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, as declared on the article page); used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the contrast in timing between fetal-onset oogenesis with decades of prophase I arrest and lifelong spermatogenesis, the single viable gamete of oogenesis against four of spermatogenesis with half the genome going to polar bodies, the difference in checkpoint stringency between the two, and that meiosis is entered by differentiated germ cells. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. The five-row comparison table in scene 4 and the invitation to predict which sex makes more segregation errors from it are the lesson's own construction.

sources.title: Tell the Difference Between Mitosis and Meiosis: Interplay Between Chromosomes, Cytoskeleton, and Cell Cycle Regulation
sources.publisher: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
sources.locator: Introduction and overview of chromosome configuration: meiosis is specialised for producing gametes while mitosis is division for somatic cells; in mitosis homologs behave independently on segregation, in meiosis they are paired and some physically connected by chiasmata; mitotic sister kinetochores are back-to-back and bi-oriented, whereas meiosis converts to side-by-side mono-orientation, essential for reductional division at meiosis I. Named components are largely from fission yeast.
sources.license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License, as declared on the article page); used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that mitosis is the division of somatic cells while meiosis is specialised for gamete production, that homologs behave independently in mitosis but are paired and connected by chiasmata in meiosis, that mitosis separates sister chromatids, and the kinetochore geometry contrast between back-to-back bi-orientation and side-by-side mono-orientation together with its role in establishing reductional division. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. Because this review's molecular account of mono-orientation rests largely on fission yeast, the lesson bounds the claim to the geometric contrast in a visible callout rather than presenting the protein-level mechanism as established in humans.

sources.title: Aneuploidy and chromosomal instability: a vicious cycle driving cellular evolution and cancer genome chaos
sources.locator: Terminology section: the human euploid genome contains 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, and a balanced number is euploid; aneuploidy is an unbalanced change in chromosome number when certain chromosomes no longer come in pairs; trisomy is a diploid genome that gained a chromosome (2N+1), trisomy 21 being an extra chromosome 21; monosomy is one that lost a chromosome (2N-1); whole-chromosome aneuploidy is distinguished from segmental aneuploidy affecting only pieces of chromosomes.
sources.license: Author manuscript deposited in PMC; used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the human euploid chromosome count of 46 in 23 pairs and the definitions of euploidy, aneuploidy, trisomy, monosomy, and the distinction between whole-chromosome and segmental aneuploidy. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. This source is a cancer-biology review and is cited here only for those definitions and the chromosome count; none of its claims about chromosomal instability in tumours is used by this lesson.

sources.title: The Colonic Crypt: Cellular Dynamics and Signaling Pathways in Homeostasis and Cancer
sources.locator: Sections on crypt architecture, renewal and cancer risk: the colon can renew every 3 to 5 days and enterocytes are replaced every 4 to 5 days; the colonic epithelium comprises crypts, tube-like pockets in the intestinal wall, with stem cells at the base responsible for self-renewal and regeneration of all mature cell types, cells differentiating as they migrate upward; cancer risk is correlated with tissues requiring a large amount of stem-cell divisions, from random mutation accumulation.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution, as declared on the article page); used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the three-to-five-day renewal of the colon and the four-to-five-day replacement of enterocytes, the crypt's architecture with a stem-cell base and differentiation up the axis, and the correlation between the number of stem-cell divisions a tissue requires and cancer risk through random mutation accumulation. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. This review was also checked for any mention of meiosis, gametes or the germ line and contains none, which is recorded in the lesson because the lesson's central contrast depends on the crypt being purely somatic.

sources.title: The cellular niche for intestinal stem cells: a team effort
sources.locator: Introductory sections on intestinal stem cells and turnover: intestinal stem cells divide about once every 24 hours; epithelial cells are continuously replaced by proliferating progenitors derived from multipotent intestinal stem cells, with a turnover time of 3 to 5 days under normal conditions; each crypt hosts 12 to 16 intestinal stem cells.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, as declared on the article page); used facts-only with no source expression reused

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that intestinal stem cells divide about once every 24 hours, the three-to-five-day epithelial turnover time, and the count of 12 to 16 intestinal stem cells per crypt. No wording, figure, table or dataset was copied or adapted. The stem-cell count is introduced to this block by this lesson rather than inherited, because no earlier lesson asserted one. The arithmetic that turns a daily division into tens of thousands of divisions over eighty years is the lesson's own.
